W1D1.inputNote: Work from the first 20 rows. Navigate with Ctrl+Arrows, select with Ctrl+Shift+Arrows.
W1D1.task: Retype these five columns for the first 20 sessions without touching the mouse.
W1D1.resultNote: Identical to the source — the exercise is the keyboard, not the answer.

W1D2.inputNote: Assistants down the side, multipliers across the top.
W1D2.task: One formula in the top-left cell, dragged across and down, fills the whole block.
W1D2.resultNote: The $ signs do the work: $A2 locks the column, B$1 locks the row.

W1D3.inputNote: Only the Workload column decides the band.
W1D3.task: Classify each session light / standard / heavy, first with nested IF, then with IFS. Both cutoffs live in cells, so changing one has to re-band every row on its own.
W1D3.resultNote: IFS reads top to bottom and stops at the first TRUE, so order the tests narrowest first.

controls.label: Light below
controls.note: Change this to 1.0 and every Band must re-read. A typed-in column will not.

controls.label: Heavy at or above
controls.note: The second cutoff. Both belong in cells, not buried in the formula.

W1D4.inputNote: Three columns are enough: Group to bucket by, Lecturer Type to filter, Workload to add up.
W1D4.task: Per Group: session count, total workload, a count of one lecturer type, and average workload. Which type gets counted comes from a cell, not from the formula.
W1D4.resultNote: Check it: the Sessions column must sum to 41, the row count of the source.

controls.label: Count which lecturer type
controls.note: Switch this to Forum and the fourth column must follow without editing a formula.

W1D5.inputNote: The Ast column repeats — 41 sessions across 21 people.
W1D5.task: Build a roster that dedupes and sorts itself, then a search cell that looks one assistant up. Typing a different code into the search cell must change the answer beside it — so the roster has to come from UNIQUE and SORT, and the lookup from XLOOKUP. Nothing typed by hand survives changing that cell.
W1D5.resultNote: Spilled, not dragged: one formula in one cell produces all 21 rows — the first 10 are shown. With HI in the search cell the lookup returns “Mobile Development”; with ZZ it must read “Not on the roster” rather than #N/A.
W1D5.formula:
=SORT(UNIQUE(tblTeaching[Ast]))
=XLOOKUP($E$1, tblTeaching[Ast], tblTeaching[Course Name], "Not on the roster")

controls.label: Search: assistant code
controls.note: Change this and the lookup beside it must follow on its own. Try ZZ, which is not on the roster — that is what XLOOKUP's if_not_found argument is for.

W1D6.inputNote: Every session with its assistant, course and workload.
W1D6.task: Build a card that answers everything about an assistant: sessions with COUNTIFS, total workload with SUMIFS, their first course with XLOOKUP, a band with IFS, and a strip of workload at 1.25x, 1.5x and 2x from one mixed-reference formula. Put a roster list beside it with SORT and UNIQUE. To get it checked, lay the card out as a table on the Answer sheet: one row per code down the first column (any assistants you like, but AB, CD and ZZ must be there), the numbers 1.25, 1.5 and 2 as the last three headers, and every row running the same formulas.

controls.label: Assistant code
controls.note: Type CD, then ZZ. Every field on the card must follow this one cell.

W1D6.resultNote: Three rows the checker requires; a row for every other assistant is fine too. AB teaches 2 sessions, 5.0 in total, and is heavy (light is under 3, standard under 4.5). CD is light at 2.0. ZZ is not on the roster, and its row says so instead of showing #N/A, which is the stretch.
W1D6.formula:
=SORT(UNIQUE(Data!A2:A42))
=COUNTIFS(Data!$A$2:$A$42, $A2)
=SUMIFS(Data!$C$2:$C$42, Data!$A$2:$A$42, $A2)
=XLOOKUP($A2, Data!$A$2:$A$42, Data!$B$2:$B$42, "not on roster")
=IF(B2=0, "not on roster", IFS(C2<3, "light", C2<4.5, "standard", TRUE, "heavy"))
=$C2*F$1

W2D1.inputNote: Convert the range to a Table first (Ctrl+T), then name it tblTeaching.
W2D1.task: Rewrite a SUMIFS using structured references instead of A1-style ranges, with the criteria read from the row label rather than typed in. Then add a row to the Table: the totals must move without you touching the formula. That is the whole point of the Table, and a hardcoded range will not do it.
W2D1.resultNote: The formula stops mentioning cell addresses, so adding rows never breaks it.

W2D2.inputNote: The allowed values come from the data itself, not from a list you type.
W2D2.task: Add list dropdowns for Group and Lecturer Type, and reject Workload outside 0 to 1.
W2D2.resultNote: Note the trap: real Workload values reach 2.5, so this rule rejects most of the sheet. That is the lesson — validation constrains new input, it does not clean existing data.
W2D2.formula: Data → Data Validation → Allow: List / Decimal

W2D3.inputNote: Two operations, in order: sort first, then filter.
W2D3.task: Sort by Group then Workload descending, then filter to VC sessions on Database Systems.
W2D3.resultNote: 2 rows survive both conditions. A filter hides rows, it does not delete them.

W2D4.inputNote: COMP6047001 — four letters, four digits, then the section.
W2D4.task: Split Course ID into department code, number and section digits — with the length of the department code read from a cell, so all three parts follow when it changes.
W2D4.resultNote: RIGHT needs LEN because the section length is not fixed — hard-coding 3 breaks on the first exception.

controls.label: Dept code length
controls.note: Set this to 3 and all three parts must shift. Typed-in values will not move.

W2D5.inputNote: SEARCH returns a position on a hit and #VALUE! on a miss — the error is the signal.
W2D5.task: Flag every course whose name contains the search term, blank otherwise. The term lives in a cell, so changing it has to re-flag the whole column.
W2D5.resultNote: Without IFERROR the column fills with #VALUE!, which is correct and unreadable. Wrapping it turns a miss into a blank.

controls.label: Search for
controls.note: Type Programming instead and the flags must move to different rows. Eyeballing will not survive it.

W2D6.inputNote: Convert this range to a Table first. Everything you add becomes a Table column.
W2D6.task: Turn the Data sheet into a Table that runs itself: dropdowns on Group and Lecturer Type, a numeric rule on Workload, Dept, Number and Section parsed out of Course ID, and a Flag column that marks courses containing the keyword in L1, with SEARCH inside IFERROR. Then type a new row under the last one and check every column fills itself in.

controls.label: Keyword
controls.note: Change it to Web and the Flag column must follow without touching a formula.

W2D6.resultNote: The first 8 of 41 rows. Only Data Structures and Database Systems carry the keyword Data. The real deliverable is a count: formula edits needed after adding a row, and the answer should be zero.
W2D6.formula:
=LEFT([@[Course ID]], 4)
=MID([@[Course ID]], 5, 4)
=RIGHT([@[Course ID]], LEN([@[Course ID]]) - 8)
=IFERROR(IF(SEARCH($L$1, [@[Course Name]]) > 0, TRUE, ""), "")
notChecked: The dropdowns on Group and Lecturer Type, and the numeric rule on Workload.
Whether a new row fills itself in.

W3D1.inputNote: Three columns that mean nothing apart and read as a label together.
W3D1.task: Build a display label from the three parts, with the separator read from a cell so changing it re-renders every label. Then use TEXTJOIN to collapse all of one assistant's classes into a single comma list.

controls.label: Separator
controls.note: Change this to " | " and every label must follow. A label typed by hand will not.

W3D1.resultNote: The first 8 of 41 labels. TEXTJOIN over the same table gives AB's classes as “BA1A, BA2A” — one cell, not one per session.

W3D2.inputNote: The roster's names, as they actually arrive.
W3D2.task: Run PROPER over TRIM on every name and compare the result with the original. Where they differ, the source was dirty; where they match, you have proved it clean rather than assumed it. Then paste a deliberately messy value into the control cell and watch the same formula fix it.

controls.label: Paste a messy value
controls.note: PROPER(TRIM()) on this must return Alfred Abner. That is the same formula the column runs.

W3D2.resultNote: The first 10 of 40. Cleaned matches Name on every row and Changed is blank throughout — 0 of 40 names needed fixing. A cleaning step that changes nothing is a passed check, not wasted work.

W3D3.inputNote: One column holding two times, separated by a hyphen.
W3D3.task: Split Time into Start and End with Text to Columns, then throw the result away and reproduce it with Flash Fill. Note which one survives new rows being added, because that is the difference that matters.
W3D3.resultNote: The first 8 of 41. Both methods produce this; neither updates when a row is added, which is the argument for doing it in Power Query later.
W3D3.formula:
Data → Text to Columns → Delimited → Other: -
Ctrl+E for Flash Fill

W3D4.task: Look a person up by their initials with INDEX and MATCH — never by counting columns. Then insert a column in the middle of the roster and confirm your formula still returns the same answer. That is the whole reason for this pairing.

controls.label: Look up which initials
controls.note: Type any code here. Try ZZ, which is not on the roster, and decide what it should say.

W3D4.resultNote: What the lookup returns for four codes. The last is deliberate: MATCH raises #N/A on a miss, so the case is not finished until that reads as something a person would want to see.

W3D5.inputNote: Every session carries an assistant, a day and a workload.
W3D5.task: Build the assistant-by-day workload matrix, then read any cell of it by naming the row and the column — one formula that answers every question of the form “how much does X carry on Y”, rather than 126 formulas.

controls.label: Which assistant
controls.note: The row half of the lookup.

controls.label: Which day
controls.note: The column half. Change either and the one formula must follow.

W3D5.resultNote: The first 8 assistants of 21. With AB and Monday in the control cells, the two-way lookup returns 2.5 — the matrix is the working, the single cell is the answer.

W3D6.inputNote: The clean roster, and beside it eight names pasted in from another system.
W3D6.task: Look up each imported name's initials with INDEX and MATCH before cleaning anything, and count the failures. Then clean the names with PROPER, TRIM and SUBSTITUTE, look them up again, and find the one that TRIM alone could not fix.
W3D6.resultNote: Before cleaning, 3 of 8 fail: Cindy Dewi has leading spaces, Fira Halim trailing ones, and Linda Maharani ends in a non-breaking space pasted from a web page. PROPER and TRIM alone reach 7 of 8, because TRIM only removes character 32, and =CODE(RIGHT(Data!C5,1)) on Linda's row returns 160. Swap it for a normal space with SUBSTITUTE first and all 8 resolve. The mixed-case names never failed, because MATCH ignores case.
W3D6.formula:
=IFNA(INDEX(Data!$A$2:$A$41, MATCH(Data!C2, Data!$B$2:$B$41, 0)), "not found")
=PROPER(TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(Data!C2, CHAR(160), " ")))
=IFNA(INDEX(Data!$A$2:$A$41, MATCH(B2, Data!$B$2:$B$41, 0)), "not found")
notChecked: The before and after failure counts you record.
The Text to Columns split and the TEXTJOIN label.

W4D1.inputNote: Workload runs 1.0 to 2.5 across the 41 sessions.
W4D1.task: Band every session by looking its workload up against a band table with XLOOKUP in next-smaller match mode. Set if_not_found so a workload the table does not cover reads as words rather than #N/A — then delete the table's first row and prove it.

controls.label: If the band table misses
controls.note: XLOOKUP's if_not_found. Delete the 0.0 row from your band table and every light session must say this.

W4D1.resultNote: The first 10 of 41, banded at 1.5 and 2.5. Zero errors is the deliverable: an #N/A anywhere means if_not_found was left out.

W4D2.inputNote: Ten distinct course names, several sharing words.
W4D2.task: Find a course from a fragment of its name using XLOOKUP in wildcard match mode. Note that it returns the first match in table order, not the best one — so try a fragment that two courses share and decide whether that is acceptable.

controls.label: Search fragment
controls.note: Wildcards on both sides. *Data* matches two courses; you get the first one in the table.

W4D2.resultNote: Four fragments and what each returns. *Data* is the interesting one — both Data Structures and Database Systems match, and only one comes back.
W4D2.formula: =XLOOKUP($E1, tblTeaching[Course Name], tblTeaching[Course ID], "no course matches", 2)

W4D3.inputNote: The same roster W3D4 used, now read with the older functions.
W4D3.task: Rebuild the W3D4 lookup with VLOOKUP, and read a day column with HLOOKUP. Then insert a column between Inisial and Name and watch exactly which of the two breaks — that is why you learned INDEX MATCH first.

controls.label: Which initials
controls.note: The VLOOKUP key.

controls.label: Which day
controls.note: The HLOOKUP key. Both must be cells, or the pair proves nothing.

W4D3.resultNote: Three lookups, each combining both functions. Same answers as INDEX MATCH would give — until a column moves.

W4D4.inputNote: Two keys, one answer: an assistant and a day together identify a session.
W4D4.task: Return the workload for a given assistant on a given day using one XLOOKUP nested inside another — the outer picking the row block, the inner picking within it. Same answer as W3D5's matrix, reached without building the matrix.

controls.label: Which assistant
controls.note: Outer key.

controls.label: Which day
controls.note: Inner key. Try Sunday, which nobody works.

W4D4.resultNote: Four pairs. The last has no session at all, which is what the nested if_not_found is for — a two-key lookup fails twice as often as a one-key one.
W4D4.formula: =XLOOKUP($F2, tblTeaching[Day], XLOOKUP($F1, tblTeaching[Ast], tblTeaching[Workload], "no session"), "no session")

W4D5.inputNote: 41 sessions across 21 assistants; the totals are what matter.
W4D5.task: Build the overloaded list with the dynamic-array set working together: UNIQUE for the roster, SUMIFS for each total, SORT to rank them, FILTER to keep only those at or over the threshold. One formula, spilling, with the threshold in a cell — raise it and the list must shorten on its own.

controls.label: Overloaded at or above
controls.note: Raise it to 5 and the list must shorten by itself. A hand-picked list will not.

W4D5.resultNote: 14 of 21 assistants carry 4.0 or more, heaviest first. Ties break alphabetically, which is SORT's own behaviour rather than something you add.
W4D5.formula:
=LET(names, UNIQUE(tblTeaching[Ast]),
     loads, SUMIFS(tblTeaching[Workload], tblTeaching[Ast], names),
     SORT(FILTER(HSTACK(names, loads), loads >= $E1), 2, -1))

W4D6.inputNote: Enough columns for four different kinds of question.
W4D6.task: Answer four questions, each with the lookup that fits it: an exact match, a partial match, a lookup that has to read left of its key, and a lookup on two conditions. Then write one line per question on why the other lookups lose.

rows.Question: Course name for session No 7
rows.Why the others lose: VLOOKUP counts columns, so inserting one returns a wrong value with no error.

rows.Question: First course whose name contains "Net"
rows.Why the others lose: An exact match on "Net" returns #N/A; a wildcard only works in match mode 2.

rows.Question: Course ID for assistant HI
rows.Why the others lose: Course ID sits left of Ast, and VLOOKUP cannot read left of its key.

rows.Question: Workload for HI on Friday
rows.Why the others lose: A one-key lookup cannot hold two criteria, and VLOOKUP has no way to combine them.

W4D6.resultNote: The Answer column is what Excel produces; the last column is what you write. Then the stretch: insert a column between Course ID and Ast, and watch a VLOOKUP written against the old layout return the wrong column with no error at all.
W4D6.formula:
=XLOOKUP(7, Data!$A$2:$A$42, Data!$C$2:$C$42)
=XLOOKUP("*Net*", Data!$C$2:$C$42, Data!$C$2:$C$42, "no match", 2)
=INDEX(Data!$B$2:$B$42, MATCH("HI", Data!$D$2:$D$42, 0))
=XLOOKUP(1, (Data!$D$2:$D$42="HI") * (Data!$E$2:$E$42="Friday"), Data!$F$2:$F$42, "no session")

W5D1.inputNote: 41 sessions; most assistants appear more than once.
W5D1.task: List every assistant once with UNIQUE, then total each one's workload with SUMIF beside it. Build it on the Answer sheet; the chart comes after, drawn from this table.
W5D1.resultNote: 21 assistants, and the totals add up to 72, the raw Workload total. If they do not, UNIQUE missed someone or SUMIF is reading the wrong range.
notChecked: The chart: a real title, an axis title, and no legend or gridlines.

W5D2.inputNote: Group down the side, Lecturer Type across the top, Workload in the cells.
W5D2.task: Build the matrix with one SUMIFS that reads its group from the row label and its lecturer type from the column header, filled right and down.
W5D2.resultNote: Every group leans VC, and G2 is the most lopsided at 12.5 to 2. Group totals run from 13.5 to 16, and the whole grid sums to 72.
notChecked: The clustered column chart and its colours.

W5D3.inputNote: The same two columns as W5D1.
W5D3.task: Rank the W5D1 summary largest first with SORT, so the ranking updates when the data does. Then chart it as horizontal bars with the biggest on top.
W5D3.resultNote: AB and HI lead at 5.0, twelve assistants sit at 4.0, and UV is last with 1.0. Tied assistants may come in either order.
notChecked: The bar chart: categories in reverse order, and data labels.

W5D4.inputNote: One column: which group each session belongs to.
W5D4.task: Count sessions per group with COUNTIF and work out each group's share of all sessions, largest first. Chart it as a pie, then as a sorted bar, and write one line on which reads faster.
W5D4.resultNote: G1 has 9 sessions (22%); the other four have 8 each (19.5%). Five near-equal slices is exactly what a pie cannot rank. Share is checked to four decimal places, so format it as a percentage however you like.
notChecked: The pie, the bar, and your one-line critique.

W5D5.task: Per day, count sessions with COUNTIF and total workload with SUMIF, Monday to Saturday in calendar order. Then a combo chart: sessions as columns, workload as a line on a secondary axis.
W5D5.resultNote: Every day has 7 sessions except Saturday with 6, yet workload drops to 7.5 on Wednesday and 6.5 on Saturday. The count alone hides the thin days, which is why the chart needs both. Keep calendar order: a line over days sorted A to Z means nothing.
notChecked: The combo chart and its secondary axis.

W5D6.inputNote: One question, four charts, all from the same summary.
W5D6.task: Chart one question, who carries the load, four ways: a ranked bar, a grouped comparison, a pie and a combo. Keep the one that answers fastest, write why each of the other three loses, then retitle the winner so its title states the answer.

rows.Why: Answers in one glance, needs no legend, and the order is the answer.
Adds a second question, VC against Forum, that nobody asked, and needs a legend to do it.
21 slices, twelve of them the same 4.0. Nobody can rank that by angle.
Puts two metrics on screen when the question named one.

W5D6.resultNote: The ranked bar wins. Its title should state the answer rather than the topic: "AB and HI carry the most load, 5.0 each against a median of 4.0", not "Workload by assistant".
W5D6.formula:
Insert > Chart, once for each of the four
Link the winner's title to a cell that states the answer

W6D1.inputNote: Enough to count assistants and find the heaviest load.
W6D1.task: Build the chart title in a cell, so it cannot go stale: "Workload by Assistant - " followed by the number of assistants and " TAs". Beside it, find the most loaded assistant with INDEX, MATCH and MAX. Then link the chart title to the title cell through the formula bar.
W6D1.resultNote: The title reads "Workload by Assistant - 21 TAs". AB and HI tie at 5.0, and MATCH returns the first one it meets, so the answer is AB. A dashboard that names only AB is hiding the tie.
W6D1.formula:
="Workload by Assistant - " & COUNTA(UNIQUE(Data!A2:A42)) & " TAs"
=LET(names, UNIQUE(Data!A2:A42), totals, SUMIF(Data!A2:A42, names, Data!B2:B42),
     INDEX(names, MATCH(MAX(totals), totals, 0)))
notChecked: Whether the chart title is linked to the cell.

W6D2.inputNote: P = Pagi, N = Normal, M = Malam. A blank is a day off.
W6D2.task: Count each shift code per weekday with COUNTIF: P, N and M down the side, Mon to Sat across, and a Total row under them. Then a stacked column chart, one stack per day.
W6D2.resultNote: Totals run 38, 30, 31, 34, 31, 34. Tuesday is the thinnest day: 10 of 40 people are off, and only 4 work Malam. Each total must equal 40 minus that day's blanks; if one comes up short, a code has a stray space or the wrong case.

W6D3.inputNote: The roster. Codes have to become numbers before a sparkline can draw them.
W6D3.task: Map each code to a number with XLOOKUP, P to 1, N to 2, M to 3, and a day off to 0, one row per assistant. Then add a line sparkline beside each row, all sharing one 0 to 3 axis.
W6D3.resultNote: 40 rows of 0 to 3. The 0s matter: without a not-found value a day off becomes #N/A and breaks the sparkline.
notChecked: The sparklines and their shared axis.

W6D4.inputNote: Every card comes from these two columns.
W6D4.task: Four KPI cards, each one a formula: total sessions, total workload, number of distinct assistants, and average load per assistant. Put the four headers in one row with the numbers under them.
W6D4.resultNote: 41 sessions, 72 workload, 21 assistants, 3.43 average. They must agree with each other: 72 / 21 = 3.43. If the average disagrees, one card is counting blank rows.
notChecked: The layout: one screen, no scrolling, one accent colour.

W6D5.inputNote: Group is the filter; the control cell picks which one.
W6D5.task: Total each assistant's workload for one group only, with the group read from the control cell. Every assistant keeps a row, so an assistant who does not teach that group shows 0.

controls.label: Group
controls.note: Make this a dropdown of G1 to G5 with Data Validation. Switch it to G1 and the column must total 16 without editing a formula.

W6D5.resultNote: For G2, eight assistants carry 14.5 between them, AB the most at 2.5, and the other 13 show 0.
notChecked: The charts redrawing when the group changes.

W6D6.inputNote: The week's pieces, assembled on one tab. The coverage view reads the Workshift roster.
W6D6.task: Put the week together on one tab: a KPI row, a coverage view, a sparkline column and a title that names the current filter. Formulas only, no pivots. Then change the Group dropdown and confirm every piece of text on the sheet moves with it.

rows.Reads from: COUNTA, SUM, COUNTA of UNIQUE, and a division

rows.Shows: Tuesday is the thinnest day, with 30 of 40 on shift
rows.Reads from: COUNTIF per day and shift code, as in W6D2

rows.Shows: One 0 to 3 line per assistant on a shared axis
rows.Reads from: The XLOOKUP code map from W6D3
A formula on the Group dropdown, so it changes with the filter

W6D6.resultNote: What each piece shows before any filter. The test is the last row: pick G2 and the title must change with it. Any text on the tab that does not move is hardcoded.

W7D1.inputNote: The full table; the pivot does the summing.
W7D1.task: Insert a PivotTable with Ast in Rows and Workload in Values, sorted largest to smallest. Check it against your W5D3 formulas before trusting it, then change a workload in the source and see what the pivot does.
W7D1.resultNote: Identical to the W5D3 ranking, with a Grand Total of 72. Now edit any workload in the source: the pivot keeps the old number until you press Alt+F5. Formulas recalculate; pivots refresh.
W7D1.formula:
Insert > PivotTable
Rows: Ast · Values: Sum of Workload
Sort Largest to Smallest on the value column

W7D2.inputNote: Course Name is there to be counted.
W7D2.task: Add a session count to the W7D1 pivot by dragging Course Name into Values. Rename both headers so a stranger can read them, set number formats inside Value Field Settings, and sort by workload.
W7D2.resultNote: Every assistant has 2 sessions except UV with 1, 41 in all. Course Name counts rather than sums because it is text. Sum of Workload cannot be renamed Workload, since that is a source column's name, so it becomes Total Workload.
W7D2.formula:
Values: Course Name (Count), renamed Sessions
Value Field Settings > Number Format on each metric

W7D3.inputNote: The W5D2 inputs, now for a pivot.
W7D3.task: Group to Rows, Lecturer Type to Columns, Workload to Values, grand totals on. This is the W5D2 matrix as a live pivot.
W7D3.resultNote: The same cells as W5D2. Pivot columns sort A to Z, so Forum comes before VC. VC carries 58 of 72, 80.6% of all load. The grid does not show the ratio inside each row; that is what W8D2's Show Values As is for.
W7D3.formula: Rows: Group · Columns: Lecturer Type · Values: Sum of Workload

W7D4.inputNote: The roster is wide, one column per day. A pivot needs it long: one row per person per day, with Day and Shift columns.
W7D4.task: Reshape the roster into Day and Shift columns, then pivot it: Day to Rows, Shift to Columns, a count to Values. Set empty cells to show 0, then add a colour scale to find the thinnest slot.
W7D4.resultNote: 198 shifts across the week. Friday Malam is the coldest cell with 3 people, and Tuesday and Thursday Malam have 4. Days off are not shifts, so they are left out. Pivot columns sort A to Z: M, N, P.
W7D4.formula:
Reshape to Day | Shift, dropping days off
Rows: Day · Columns: Shift · Values: Count of Inisial
PivotTable Options > For empty cells show: 0

W7D5.inputNote: Add a Sessions column of 1s to the source; a calculated field can only use source fields.
W7D5.task: Add a calculated field that divides workload by sessions, beside the raw sums. Then compare its Grand Total with the average of the rows above it.
W7D5.resultNote: Most assistants average 2.0 per session. The Grand Total reads 1.7561, which is 72 / 41, while the average of the 21 row values is 1.738. A calculated field sums its inputs across the whole table first and divides after. Neither number is wrong, they answer different questions, and the pivot does not say which one you got.
W7D5.formula:
Source: Sessions = 1 on every row
Fields, Items & Sets > Calculated Field: Avg per Session = Workload / Sessions

W7D6.task: Rebuild four earlier answers as pivots on one tab, time yourself, and check each against its formula original.
W7D6.resultNote: Every pivot must match its original exactly. If one does not, it is filtering something you did not intend, usually a stale cached item. The answer a formula still does better is any number inside a sentence or a KPI card, because a pivot cell moves when the pivot reshapes.
W7D6.formula: One tab, four PivotTables from the same source

W8D1.inputNote: Six days to fold into two bands.
W8D1.task: Pivot workload by Day, then group Monday to Wednesday as Early week and Thursday to Saturday as Late week.
W8D1.resultNote: 36.5 early against 35.5 late, still 72 in total. Grouping reshapes and never filters, so a Grand Total that moves means something was excluded. If Group is greyed out, the field holds a blank or a stray text value.
W8D1.formula:
Select Monday to Wednesday > right-click > Group, rename Early week
Repeat for Thursday to Saturday

W8D2.task: Show Workload three ways in one pivot: as it is, as % of Column Total, and ranked largest to smallest.
W8D2.resultNote: AB and HI each carry 6.9%. Pivot ranks are dense: the two tied at 5.0 are both 1, the twelve at 4.0 are all 2, and UV is 5. RANK.EQ would put the 4.0s at 3, so do not mix the two. The % column must total 100%.
W8D2.formula:
Add Workload to Values three times
Show Values As > % of Column Total
Show Values As > Rank Largest to Smallest, base field Ast

W8D3.inputNote: Group and Lecturer Type become slicers.
W8D3.task: Add Group and Lecturer Type slicers to the assistant pivot, style them as buttons, then set Group to G2 and Lecturer Type to VC.
W8D3.resultNote: Six assistants are left, carrying 12.5, with AB the most at 2.5. Assistants with no G2 VC sessions disappear rather than showing 0. Tick Hide items with no data so each slicer stops offering choices that lead nowhere.
W8D3.formula:
PivotTable Analyze > Insert Slicer > Group, Lecturer Type
Slicer Settings > Hide items with no data

W8D4.inputNote: Two pivots from the same source.
W8D4.task: Build a workload-by-assistant pivot and a workload-by-day pivot from the same source, then connect one Group slicer to both with Report Connections. Set it to G3.
W8D4.resultNote: The assistant pivot shows 8 rows and the day pivot 6, and both total 13.5. That agreement is the test. A pivot missing from Report Connections was built on its own cache: copy the first pivot and change its fields instead of inserting a new one.
W8D4.formula: Right-click the slicer > Report Connections > tick both pivots

W8D5.inputNote: The roster with Gen, the cohort each assistant joined in.
W8D5.task: Reshape the roster to one row per person per day (Inisial, Gen, Day, Code), drop the days off, then pivot: Gen to Rows, Code to Columns, a count to Values.
W8D5.resultNote: Every cohort has 8 people, so a full week is 48 shifts. The totals are 39, 40, 38, 40 and 41, so 25-1 has the most days off (10) and 26-1 the fewest (7). Leave days off out: filling them with N to make the numbers tidy would invent coverage.
W8D5.formula:
Data > From Table/Range > select the day columns > Unpivot Columns
Rows: Gen · Columns: Code · Values: Count of Inisial

W8D6.inputNote: Everything on the tab reads this one source.
W8D6.task: Put a grouped time band, a percent of total and a ranking on one tab, wire them all to one Group slicer, and compare the tab with and without the slicer.
W8D6.resultNote: Under G1 the early and late bands fall to 7.5 and 8.5. The share pivot re-bases to the filtered total: AB is 6.9% of everything but 15.6% of G1. Nothing on screen says which total that is, so the title has to name the filter.
W8D6.formula: Right-click the slicer > Report Connections > tick every pivot on the tab

W9D1.task: Build a PivotChart from the group pivot, attach a Lecturer Type slicer, and set it to Forum.
W9D1.resultNote: Forum carries 14 of the 72, from 2.0 in G2 to 3.5 in G1. The chart and the pivot redraw in the same refresh, so they cannot disagree. Hide the field buttons once the layout is settled.
W9D1.formula:
PivotTable Analyze > PivotChart
PivotChart Analyze > Field Buttons > Hide All

W9D2.inputNote: The teaching table. Gen and each day's shift come from the Workshift roster, as a Table named Workshift.
W9D2.task: Bring Gen into the teaching table with XLOOKUP on Ast, with "unknown" for a code that is not on the roster. Bring in the shift that assistant works on the session's day too, then pivot workload by Gen and Shift.
W9D2.resultNote: Three cohorts teach: 24-1 carries 30, 24-2 carries 27 and 25-1 carries 15. Every code matched, so there is no unknown column here; change one Ast to ZZ to see it appear. The off column is the finding: 9.5 of workload falls on days the roster says those assistants are off.
W9D2.formula:
=XLOOKUP([@Ast], Workshift[Inisial], Workshift[Gen], "unknown")
=LET(s, XLOOKUP([@Ast], Workshift[Inisial], XLOOKUP(LEFT([@Day], 3), Workshift[#Headers], Workshift), "unknown"),
     IF(s = "", "off", s))

W9D3.inputNote: The joined teaching table, with Gen added in W9D2.
W9D3.task: Assemble a one-screen dashboard from the joined table: KPI cards, three pivots, and slicers on Group, Gen and Lecturer Type, all connected. Then clear every slicer and check the baseline.
W9D3.resultNote: Cleared, the dashboard must read 41 sessions, 72 workload and 21 assistants, the same as the single-file figures, since a lookup adds no rows. With Gen set to 24-2 it reads 16, 27 and 8.
W9D3.formula: Slicers: Group, Gen, Lecturer Type · Report Connections: every pivot

W9D4.inputNote: The teaching table and the roster, both added to the Data Model.
W9D4.task: Add both tables to the Data Model, relate Ast to Inisial, and build the cohort pivot with Gen from the roster and Workload from the teaching table, with no helper columns.
W9D4.resultNote: The same totals as W9D2: 30, 27 and 15, with nothing copied between tables. If every row repeats 72, the relationship is missing or reversed. Inisial is the one side, 40 unique codes, and Ast the many side.
W9D4.formula:
Insert > PivotTable > Add this data to the Data Model, for both tables
Data > Relationships: Teaching[Ast] to Workshift[Inisial]

W9D5.task: One tab, four pivots, one per operations question, with slicers on Group and Day connected to all four, laid out to read without scrolling.

rows.Question: Who is overloaded?
rows.Answer: AB and HI, 5.0 each, against a median of 4.0.

W9D5.resultNote: The four answers the tab has to make obvious. With every slicer cleared it must read 41 sessions, 72 workload and 21 assistants. A dashboard that cannot return to that baseline will eventually be quoted while filtered.
W9D5.formula: Four PivotTables · Slicers: Group, Day · Report Connections: all four
